evidence: chapter-08.md Fig 8.1 caption: 'The resource stack runs from the smallest/fastest/closest resource (registers, tensor cores, on-chip SRAM) to the largest/slower/farther (HBM, GPU interconnect, other GPUs).' Same caption: 'compute, memory and interconnect are separate groups within this stack, not levels of one ladder.' Follow-up paragraph: 'Read this ladder together with the roofline:'. One smallest→largest ordering placing tensor cores between registers and SRAM coexists with the 'not levels of one ladder' disclaimer and the 'ladder' label — internal tension present in current source.
fix_instruction: Restructure figure and caption into separate groups (compute units / memory hierarchy / interconnect); if a ladder remains, restrict it to the memory hierarchy and stop calling the combined set one ladder.

evidence: chapter-08.md: 'a kernel's horizontal position (FLOP/byte) is set by its arithmetic intensity — not by where the work sits on this resource stack.' Same paragraph: 'A kernel is compute-bound when its arithmetic intensity sits above the ridge point (keeping data on-chip raises that intensity)' and 'it follows from where the model's weights and the KV cache happen to be resident, and how much of the computation a kernel can keep on-chip.' The flat denial conflicts with both follow-ons in the same paragraph.
fix_instruction: Rewrite: 'the horizontal position is set by arithmetic intensity, which depends on the kernel's data reuse and tiling — including how much data it keeps on-chip — not merely on the nominal memory level.'

evidence: chapter-08.md §2: 'FLOPs are like the total distance of a trip: they tell us how much work the request requires, not how fast the system can cover it. ... if the arithmetic intensity is below the ridge, adding more FLOPs won't help because we are waiting for data.' The same paragraph defines FLOPs as work; the book uses TFLOPS/FLOP/s for rates ('989 TFLOPS', '346 TFLOPS'). 'Adding more FLOPs' literally means more work, not more compute throughput — terminology drift confirmed.
fix_instruction: Replace with 'adding more compute throughput (FLOP/s) won't help' (or 'more compute capacity'); keep FLOPs for work counts.

evidence: chapter-08.md §1 heading: '### A resource model survives a backend change; an implementation may not'; body: 'In PyTorch, `torch.xpu` names the Intel GPU device backend (... pinned revision `5c48869`)...' followed by the hpu/NPU/Gaudi inventory with pinned links. The vendor inventory is the evidence for the section's stated principle (device API availability ≠ operator support ≠ sustained performance); length and placement are editorial choices, and the sources are pinned/dated rather than loose.

evidence: chapter-08.md: 'For decode, the per-token FLOP cost is the same ~140 GFLOP, but the arithmetic intensity drops sharply.' Using the book's own attention term (4·n_layers·L²·d, with d = 8,192 and 80 layers per its table '4 ×80 ×9,200² ×8,192'): per decode token 4×80×9,200×8,192 = 24.1×10⁹ FLOP ⇒ 140 + 24.1 ≈ 164 GFLOP/token, not ~140. The KV-read caveat adds bytes only ('omits the per-sequence KV re-read (~24 GB...)'), no attention FLOPs — arithmetic verified.
fix_instruction: Change to 'the parameterized linear FLOP cost is the same ~140 GFLOP; decode attention adds a context-dependent term (~24 GFLOP/token at 9.2K)' and use the total in any full decode roofline.

evidence: chapter-08.md: 'Any KV/output-projection reads are a separate, smaller term on top, not a second full weight footprint.' Preceding: 'A 70B FP16 weight matrix is 70 ×10⁹ × 2 B = 140 GB' — the full parameter set, which includes the output projection/LM head. Listing output-projection reads as a separate term on top of the 140 GB weight stream double-counts a weight already in the footprint; only KV reads are genuinely separate.
fix_instruction: Rewrite: 'Any KV-cache reads are a separate term on top; the output projection is already included in the 140 GB weight footprint.'

chapter-08.md: 'the arithmetic intensity of a mature attention kernel sits near or above this ridge, meaning the kernel is compute-saturated rather than bandwidth-starved once the batch is large enough.' The book's own Fig 8.2 caption: 'Prefill sits far above the ridge — its arithmetic intensity is set by the sequence length (weights read once, reused across all tokens)'. For attention, batch multiplies FLOPs and bytes alike (FlashAttention intensity ∝ L, unchanged by batch), so the conditioning variable in the quoted sentence is wrong per the caption's own account.
fix_instruction: Replace 'once the batch is large enough' with 'once the sequence is long enough (attention intensity scales with L; at the canonical 9.2K it sits far above the ridge)'.
